reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Overview of spray applications of asphalt material as an economical maintenance and repair method for flexible pavements. Spray applications improve pavement condition and extend pavement life but do not add structural strength. The chapter covers prime coats, tack coats, fog seals, and rejuvenators.
sections.body: "Spray application" is a term used to describe many different types of asphalt applications. An economical maintenance and repair method for flexible pavements is accomplished using spray applications of an asphalt material. When properly constructed, asphalt spray applications are economical as well as long lasting and are beneficial in treating or improving the pavement condition and increasing the life of the pavement. Where additional thickness is needed to increase the structural strength of pavements, spray applications are not considered helpful because they don't contribute the structural strength. The different types of spray applications discussed in this chapter are prime coats, tack coats, and fog seals and rejuvenators. The main cause for concern with fog seals and rejuvenators is reduced skid resistance, discussed in sections 3-4 and 3-5. The amount of application is greater in lower-trafficked areas, such as pavement shoulders, the outer edges of runway and taxi pavements, and parking areas. Application rates are greatest where high-speed traffic is not expected. Due to a possible decrease in skid resistance, obtain approval from the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) or their designated representative prior to using fog seals and rejuvenators.
key_points: Spray applications are economical maintenance/repair treatments for flexible pavements, not structural thickness additions.
The four spray application types covered are prime coats, tack coats, fog seals, and rejuvenators.
Fog seals and rejuvenators can reduce skid resistance and require DWG approval before use.
Application rates are typically higher on low-speed/low-traffic areas (shoulders, runway/taxiway edges, parking) than high-speed traffic areas.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever selecting or specifying a spray-applied asphalt treatment for flexible pavement maintenance or construction.

sections.title: Prime Coat
sections.summary: A prime coat is a low-viscosity liquid asphalt applied to an unbound base course before HMA placement, to prevent lateral movement, waterproof the base, and promote adhesion of the pavement. It must penetrate the base and be allowed to cure before construction traffic.
sections.body: Asphalt prime coat consists of a low-viscosity liquid asphalt material applied by a pressure distributor to an unbound base course before placement of a HMA pavement. The purposes of the prime coat are to prevent lateral movement of the unbound base during pavement construction, to waterproof during pavement construction, and to form a tight, tough base to which an asphalt pavement adheres. The prime material must penetrate into the unbound base and fill the void spaces. A completed unbound base is susceptible to serious damage from rain, wind, and traffic, and a prime coat is insurance against this water and traffic damage. Apply prime coat material to a dust-free, unbound base as soon as the base has been thoroughly compacted and before construction or other traffic loosens surface material. For best penetration of emulsions, application of water (saturation or ponding) improves wetability and penetration. If an asphalt layer follows in less than 7 days after base compaction, priming is not mandatory (though preferred); if construction does not occur for at least 7 days, the compacted base is primed. A prime coat is generally allowed to cure for 48 hours to withstand construction traffic, with cool or wet weather increasing the required time. Local conditions, local experience, the type of base material, and the type of prime coat material available are all considered when deciding on prime coat application.
key_points: Prime coat prevents lateral movement of the unbound base, waterproofs it during construction, and forms a tight base for pavement adhesion.
Priming is optional if HMA placement follows within 7 days of base compaction, but mandatory (preferred) if construction is delayed 7+ days.
Typical cure time is 48 hours before construction traffic; cool or wet weather increases this.
Water saturation/ponding before applying emulsion prime improves wetability and penetration.
sections.applicability: Applies to preparation of an unbound base course prior to placement of a hot-mix asphalt pavement layer.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Recommended prime coat materials are low-viscosity cutback (liquid) and emulsified asphalts, selected considering air temperature, humidity, base void content, curing time, environmental restrictions, and material availability.
sections.body: Use low-viscosity asphalt material as prime material, with selection of type and grade given careful consideration. Items considered in selecting the priming material include: air temperature, humidity, void content of the base course, curing time of the prime material, environmental restrictions, and available materials.
key_points: Selection factors: air temperature, humidity, base course void content, curing time, environmental restrictions, material availability.
Prime material must be low-viscosity to penetrate the base course.
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing the type and grade of asphalt material for a prime coat.

sections.title: Asphalt
sections.summary: Selection considerations for the low-viscosity asphalt material used as prime, including air temperature, humidity, base void content, curing time, environmental restrictions, and material availability, drive the choice of cutback or emulsion type.
sections.body: Use low-viscosity asphalt material as prime material, but ensure the selection of type and grade is given consideration. These following items are considered in selecting the priming material: air temperature; humidity; void content of the base course; curing time of the prime material; environmental restrictions; available materials.
key_points: Prime asphalt selection weighs air temperature, humidity, base void content, curing time, environmental restrictions, and availability.
Low viscosity is essential so the prime material can penetrate the base.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the specific asphalt material used for priming an unbound base course.

sections.title: Prime Coats
sections.summary: Recommended priming materials are emulsified asphalts and cutback (liquid) asphalts, per Table 3-1's recommended types/grades. Open-textured (high-void) bases prime easily; tight (low-void) surfaces need less-viscous cutbacks such as RC-70, MC-30, MC-70, or SC-70 to avoid leaving a slippage-causing film.
sections.body: Recommended priming materials include emulsified asphalts and cutback (liquid) asphalt; Table 3-1 shows the recommended types and grades (cutbacks SC-70, SC-250, MC-30, MC-70, MC-250, RC-70, RC-250; emulsions SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, CSS-1h). A prime coat works only if it penetrates into the base course. Open-textured (high void content) bases are primed easily, but a tight surface (low voids) cannot be penetrated readily; in cases of low voids, consider less viscous cutbacks such as RC-70, MC-30, MC-70, and SC-70. If penetration does not occur, an asphalt film is left on the surface of the base, causing slippage of the bituminous surface during and after construction. Use caution with RC-70 or RC-250 because the solvent evaporates rapidly or is absorbed by base course fines, leaving a surface film. Undiluted emulsions cause film problems on tight base surfaces; when emulsions are used, dilute 1 part water to 1 part emulsion. Generally, cutback asphalts penetrate better than asphalt emulsions, but many areas restrict cutback use, so many suppliers produce emulsions specially formulated for prime coats.
key_points: Table 3-1 lists recommended cutback grades (SC-70/250, MC-30/70/250, RC-70/250) and emulsion grades (SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, CSS-1h) for prime coats.
Tight, low-void base surfaces need less-viscous cutbacks (RC-70, MC-30, MC-70, SC-70) to penetrate rather than film over.
Emulsions used for prime coat are typically diluted 1 part water to 1 part emulsion.
Cutbacks generally penetrate better than emulsions but face environmental-restriction limits on use.
Failure to penetrate leaves an asphalt film that causes slippage of the bituminous surface.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting between cutback and emulsion prime coat grades based on base course void content and site conditions.

sections.title: Influence of Weather
sections.summary: Weather affects the choice of prime material: emulsions depend on water evaporation to cure, so low temperature or high humidity slows or stops curing, while cutbacks are less weather-dependent; among cutbacks, rapid-curing (RC) grades cure faster than medium/slow-curing (MC/SC) grades in cold weather.
sections.body: Weather influences the choice of the correct priming materials. Since emulsions are dependent on the evaporation of water for curing, low temperature or high humidity slow or stop the curing process. Cutbacks are not as dependent on weather conditions as emulsions. In cold weather, however, the rapid-curing cutbacks (RCs) cure quicker than the slower curing cutbacks (MCs and SCs).
key_points: Emulsion curing depends on water evaporation, so it slows in cold or humid weather.
Cutbacks are less weather-dependent than emulsions overall.
In cold weather, RC cutbacks cure faster than MC or SC cutbacks.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a prime coat material for cold, humid, or otherwise weather-constrained construction conditions.

sections.title: Considerations for Use of Cutbacks
sections.summary: Cutback prime materials are widely available but face increasing environmental, safety, flammability, and cost pressure that has driven a shift toward emulsion prime coats, which must be diluted with water and protected from freezing, settling, and breaking.
sections.body: Cutback materials are available in locations throughout the United States and the world. Environmental, safety, and cost considerations have led to increased use of emulsions as prime coat materials. Environmental restrictions, under certain conditions, have begun to limit the use of cutback prime coat materials. This plus concerns about flammability and the cost of cutbacks have led to increased use of asphalt emulsion prime coats. Dilute asphalt emulsions with water before applying as a prime coat, and exercise handling and storage considerations to prevent freezing, settling, and breaking.
key_points: Environmental restrictions increasingly limit cutback prime coat use.
Flammability and cost concerns favor emulsion prime coats over cutbacks.
Asphalt emulsions must be diluted with water and protected from freezing, settling, and breaking during storage.
sections.applicability: Applies when weighing cutback versus emulsion prime coat materials for environmental compliance and cost.

sections.title: Application Rate
sections.summary: Prime coats are typically applied at 0.45 to 1.13 liters per square meter (0.10 to 0.25 gallons per square yard) of residual asphalt; the optimum rate depends on base plasticity index, fines content and nature, surface tightness, and moisture, and should be set by field trial test sections.
sections.body: Prime coats are usually applied in quantities of 0.45 to 1.13 liters per square meter (0.10 to 0.25 gallons per square yard) of residual asphalt. The optimum amount of prime is highly dependent on the plasticity index of the base material, the amount of fines in the base, the nature of the fines, the tightness of the surface, and the moisture content of the base; therefore, determine the optimum amount of prime required by field trial. Test sections at various application rates are recommended for determining the optimum amount of prime. After 48 hours of curing, if there is free or excess bitumen on the surface or if the base continues to appear shiny, the base is probably overprimed. Generally, the prime is absorbed into the base within 2 to 3 hours. When excessive prime is used, the surplus probably is absorbed into the overlying asphalt layers, contributing to pavement slippage or rutting. Where excessive prime is applied, blot the excess with an application of clean fine sand or mineral dust. The ideal end result is to obtain maximum penetration without leaving free prime on the surface.
key_points: Typical prime coat application rate: 0.45-1.13 L/sq m (0.10-0.25 gal/sq yd) of residual asphalt.
Optimum rate depends on base plasticity index, fines content/nature, surface tightness, and moisture; set by field trial test sections.
Prime is generally absorbed into the base within 2 to 3 hours.
Excess (unabsorbed, shiny) prime after 48 hours indicates overpriming; blot excess with clean fine sand or mineral dust.
Overpriming risks pavement slippage or rutting from excess prime absorbed into overlying asphalt layers.
sections.applicability: Applies when setting the target application rate (gal/sq yd) for a prime coat on a given base course.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Primed surfaces should be lightly broomed of loose material before application; a light water application before priming helps prevent "freckling." The primer must be applied uniformly by a calibrated pressure distributor at the required rate and temperature, curing within 48 hours.
sections.body: Lightly broom surfaces to be primed that contain appreciable amounts of loose material or are dusty. A dusty surface causes prime to "freckle," that is, have areas with no prime and adjacent areas with drops of excess prime. A light application of water just before applying the prime aids in reducing freckles and getting good distribution of the prime. Ensure the primer is uniformly applied with a pressure distributor at the required application rate and at the specified temperature for the asphalt used. The minimum curing time varies according to the grade and type of asphalt being used, the nature of the base, the temperature, and the humidity, but curing takes place within 48 hours.
key_points: Broom loose material/dust from the base before priming to avoid "freckling."
A light water application before priming reduces freckling and improves prime distribution.
Prime must be applied uniformly by a pressure distributor at the specified rate and temperature.
Curing generally completes within 48 hours, varying with asphalt grade/type, base nature, temperature, and humidity.
sections.applicability: Applies to field placement procedures immediately before and during prime coat spraying.

sections.title: Control
sections.summary: Prime coat quality control requires calibrating and checking the pressure distributor for the specified application rate (per ASTM D2995) and ensuring uniform nozzle condition, size, and angle, plus correct spray bar height to avoid streaking.
sections.body: Since prime coat material is applied with a pressure distributor, calibrate and check the distributor for the specified application rate before applying the prime. ASTM D2995 offers a method for determining the application rate of bituminous distributors. In addition, ensure all nozzles are free and open, the same size, and to the same angle in reference to the spray bar to produce a uniform fan of prime. The height of the spray bar above the surface is important because a bar too high or too low gives an unequal application across the spray bar, causing streaking. Ensure the height of the spray bar is such that a double or triple lap of the spray fan is obtained.
key_points: Calibrate and check the pressure distributor's application rate per ASTM D2995 before priming.
Nozzles must be free, open, uniform size, and at a uniform angle to produce a uniform spray fan.
Correct spray bar height (giving a double or triple lap of the spray fan) prevents streaking.
sections.applicability: Applies to quality control checks on the pressure distributor before and during prime coat application.

sections.title: Tack Coat
sections.summary: A tack coat is a light asphalt application to an existing paved surface immediately before placing the next pavement layer, applied by pressure distributor to bond the two layers. It is always required between a new asphalt mixture and an underlying bound layer (HMA or PCC).
sections.body: A tack coat is a light application of asphalt material to an existing paved surface immediately prior to placing the next pavement layer or course. The purpose of the tack coat is to provide a bond between the two pavement layers. The tack coat is applied by pressure distributor to cleaned surfaces, in a light and uniform application.
key_points: Tack coat bonds a new pavement layer to an existing paved (bound) surface.
Applied by pressure distributor in a light, uniform coat to a cleaned surface.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever placing a new asphalt layer on top of an existing paved (bound) surface such as HMA or PCC.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Emulsions are the common tack coat material (used undiluted), though cutbacks and asphalt cements are also used; Table 3-2 gives recommended materials and spray temperatures. A tack coat is always required over a bound layer such as HMA or PCC.
sections.body: Emulsions are common types of asphalt material used as tack, but cutbacks and asphalt cements are also used. For tack coats, the asphalt emulsion is not to be diluted. Obtain the correct spraying viscosities (temperatures) for the type of material used. Recommended tack coat materials and spray application temperatures are shown in Table 3-2. Cutbacks and emulsions are sprayed at low temperatures, but asphalt cements require considerable heating to reach a viscosity for spraying. A tack coat is always to be used when adding an asphalt mixture on top of a bound layer such as HMA or Portland cement concrete (PCC). In cold weather, cutbacks are used with less concern than emulsions, though the same availability concerns noted for prime coats apply. Use of an emulsion requires consideration of weather conditions, storage and handling requirements, and curing time. Ensure all tack coats are completely cured before placing the new pavement layer.
key_points: Tack coat emulsions are used undiluted (unlike prime coat emulsions).
Table 3-2 lists recommended tack coat materials (cutbacks, emulsions, asphalt cements) and their spray application temperatures.
Asphalt cements require considerable heating to reach sprayable viscosity, unlike cutbacks/emulsions.
A tack coat is always required over a bound layer (HMA or PCC) before placing a new asphalt mixture.
tables: Table 3-2: Tack Coat Materials and Spray Application Temperatures
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the tack coat material type and spray temperature for a given bound underlying surface.

sections.title: Application Rate
sections.summary: Tack coats are usually applied at 0.23 to 0.68 liters per square meter (0.05 to 0.15 gallons per square yard) of residual asphalt, adjusted to field conditions; light applications are preferred since heavy applications cause slippage/bleeding, but omitting tack coat also causes slippage.
sections.body: Tack coats are usually applied in quantities of 0.23 to 0.68 liter per square meter (0.05 to 0.15 gallon per square yard) of residual asphalt, but adjust the exact quantities to suit field conditions. Light applications are preferred since heavy applications cause serious pavement slippage and bleeding problems; however, failure to use any tack coat also causes pavement slippage problems.
key_points: Typical tack coat application rate: 0.23-0.68 L/sq m (0.05-0.15 gal/sq yd) of residual asphalt.
Heavy tack applications cause slippage and bleeding; no tack coat at all also causes slippage.
tables: Table 3-2: Tack Coat Materials and Spray Application Temperatures
sections.applicability: Applies when setting the target application rate (gal/sq yd) for a tack coat between two pavement layers.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Tack coats are applied to clean, dust-free bound surfaces immediately before overlay placement, at a temperature giving a viscosity of 10-60 seconds Saybolt Furol (20-120 centistokes), and must be fully cured (tacky) before the overlying layer is placed.
sections.body: Apply tack coats to clean, dust-free asphalt pavement courses prior to placement of the overlying pavement layer, immediately before placement of the overlay; therefore, unless an asphalt cement is used, allow the tack coat time to cure. A tack coat is required on a base course when the prime coat on that surface has been subjected to construction traffic or other traffic. Use a pressure distributor to apply tack coats at an application temperature that produces a viscosity between 10 and 60 seconds, Saybolt Furol, or between 20 and 120 centistokes, kinematic viscosity; suggested spray application temperatures are shown in Table 3-2. When an even or uniform coating is not obtained, improved coverage is possible by making several passes over the freshly applied tack coat with a pneumatic-tired roller, though steps should still be taken to ensure uniform application from the distributor. Ensure the tack coat is completely cured (volatiles or water evaporated) before the overlying layer is placed; a properly cured surface feels tacky. Plan work so the amount of tack coat placed equals the amount required for one day of operation, and keep nonessential traffic off the tack coat. Tack-free-when-cured products exist to prevent tracking; guidance is provided in UFGS 32 12 13.
key_points: Tack coat must be applied at a temperature giving 10-60 seconds Saybolt Furol viscosity (20-120 centistokes kinematic).
A tack coat is required on a base course if its prime coat was subjected to construction traffic.
Tack coat must fully cure (feel tacky, volatiles/water evaporated) before overlying layer placement.
Tack-free-when-cured products (UFGS 32 12 13) prevent truck tracking of tack material.
Place only one day's worth of tack coat at a time and keep nonessential traffic off it.
tables: Table 3-2: Tack Coat Materials and Spray Application Temperatures
sections.applicability: Applies to field placement and curing verification of a tack coat before overlay paving.

sections.title: Control
sections.summary: Tack coat application control follows the same distributor calibration and nozzle-check procedures described for prime coat control in section 3-2.2/3-2.4.
sections.body: The control of tack coat application is the same as that for prime coat application, as discussed in paragraph 3-2.2 (distributor calibration per ASTM D2995 and nozzle uniformity checks).
key_points: Tack coat control mirrors prime coat control: calibrated distributor, ASTM D2995 method, uniform nozzles.
sections.applicability: Applies to quality control of tack coat application, following the same procedure as prime coat control.

sections.title: Fog Seals
sections.summary: A fog seal is a light spray application of diluted emulsified asphalt to an existing pavement surface to maintain old pavements, reduce raveling, waterproof, and extend service life on lightly-trafficked pavements; it can reduce skid resistance and air voids, and requires 12-24 hours pavement closure to cure.
sections.body: A fog seal is a light spray application of diluted emulsified asphalt to an existing asphalt pavement surface. Fog seals are used to maintain old pavements, reduce raveling, waterproof, and in general extend the life of existing pavements. Fog seals are good for treating pavements that carry little or no traffic; however, there are several considerations when using fog seals: the pavement skid resistance is possibly reduced; the pavement air voids or permeability is possibly reduced; and the pavement must be closed to traffic for 12 to 24 hours to allow curing of the seal material.
key_points: Fog seals maintain old pavements, reduce raveling, waterproof, and extend pavement life.
Best suited to pavements with little or no traffic due to reduced skid resistance.
Fog seals can reduce pavement air voids/permeability.
Pavement closure of 12-24 hours is required for the seal material to cure.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a light maintenance seal for an aged, low-traffic asphalt pavement surface.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Fog seals now primarily use slow-setting asphalt emulsions (SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, CSS-1h) rather than the cutbacks historically used, to allow maximum asphalt penetration; rejuvenators are a related proprietary product family covered in section 3-5.
sections.body: In the past, asphalt emulsions and cutbacks were used for fog seals, but in recent years, the materials used are emulsions and rejuvenators. The emulsions often used are SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, and CSS-1h. Use only slow-setting emulsions, to allow for maximum penetration of the asphalt into the pavement. Several products are marketed as rejuvenators; they are proprietary products and their use is discussed in section 3-5.
key_points: Fog seal materials are now primarily slow-setting emulsions (SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, CSS-1h) and rejuvenators.
Slow-setting emulsions are used specifically to maximize asphalt penetration into the pavement.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting the emulsion grade for a fog seal treatment.

sections.title: Application Rate
sections.summary: Fog seal application/dilution rate varies with pavement absorption characteristics, typically 0.14 to 0.36 liters per square meter (0.03 to 0.08 gallons per square yard of residual asphalt); test sections set the best rate, and normal emulsion dilution is 1 part emulsion to 1 part water.
sections.body: The application and dilution rate for fog seal varies with the absorption characteristics of the existing pavement surface. Rates vary between 0.14 to 0.36 liters per square meter (0.03 to 0.08 gallons per square yard of residual asphalt). Place test sections on the pavement to determine the best application rate. Adjust the application rate so that the pavement does not become slick or unstable and does not have excess free material on the surface after curing 12 to 24 hours. Asphalt emulsions are applied at full strength or are diluted as much as 1 part emulsion to 5 parts or more of water; however, normal application dilution is 1 part emulsion to 1 part water. Evaluate the amount of dilution for each job using a test section.
key_points: Typical fog seal application rate: 0.14-0.36 L/sq m (0.03-0.08 gal/sq yd) of residual asphalt.
Normal emulsion dilution for fog seal is 1 part emulsion to 1 part water (up to 1:5 or more possible).
Application rate is set via test sections to avoid a slick/unstable surface or excess free material after 12-24 hours curing.
sections.applicability: Applies when setting the target application/dilution rate for a fog seal on a given pavement surface.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Fog seal is applied with a calibrated pressure distributor to a cleaned surface at ambient temperature above 4.5 C (40 F), with warmer temperatures preferred for faster breaking/curing; excess seal material is blotted with clean sand.
sections.body: Use only a pressure distributor that has been calibrated to deliver the fog seal at the specified rate to apply the seal material. Clean all surfaces to which the seal is applied. Apply the fog seal when the ambient temperature is above 4.5 degrees C (40 degrees F), but warmer temperatures are preferable because the material breaks and cures faster. The seal material is applied to a damp pavement if the dilution material is water, but ensure the pavement is not too wet or the seal does not break properly and does not penetrate into the pavement. Blot excess seal left on the surface with clean sand and broom.
key_points: Minimum application temperature for fog seal is 4.5 C (40 F); warmer temperatures give faster breaking/curing.
Pavement may be damp (if diluted with water) but not too wet, or the seal fails to break and penetrate.
Excess fog seal is blotted with clean sand and broomed.
sections.applicability: Applies to field placement conditions (temperature, surface moisture) for fog seal application.

sections.title: Rejuvenation
sections.summary: Rejuvenation is the spray application of a proprietary material to soften/restore an aged asphalt binder, extending pavement life; effective before block cracking or substantial raveling occurs, typically needed 3-6 years after placement, but restricted on runways without fine aggregate cover due to reduced friction.
sections.body: Rejuvenation is the spray application of a material on an asphalt surface for the purpose of rejuvenating an aged asphalt cement binder. This rejuvenation is intended to extend the life of the asphalt pavement by softening or rejuvenating the surface asphalt toward the properties it had shortly after construction. The application of a rejuvenator is effective when the pavement has not aged to the point at which block cracking or substantial raveling has occurred. Depending on the climatic conditions, pavement rejuvenation is required within 3 to 6 years after placement. Rejuvenators are spray applied to the pavement surface and allowed to penetrate into the pavement. Rejuvenators are not to be used on runways without fine aggregate cover due to their tendency to reduce the surface friction. Obtain approval from the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) or their designated representative prior to the use of rejuvenators or rejuvenator-sealers on airfields.
key_points: Rejuvenation softens/restores an aged asphalt binder toward its as-constructed properties, extending pavement life.
Most effective before block cracking or substantial raveling occurs; typically needed 3-6 years after placement.
Rejuvenators are prohibited on runways without fine aggregate cover due to reduced surface friction.
DWG approval is required before using rejuvenators or rejuvenator-sealers on airfields.
sections.applicability: Applies to maintenance treatment of an aged asphalt pavement surface not yet exhibiting block cracking or substantial raveling.

sections.title: Testing
sections.summary: The viscosity test is more effective than the penetration test at detecting rejuvenator-induced changes in asphalt properties; the dynamic shear rheometer (DSR) test, using the phase angle parameter (more statistically consistent than G*), is also used and requires less asphalt.
sections.body: Test results have shown that the viscosity test is effective in determining a change in asphalt properties compared to a penetration test. The viscosity test identifies changes in asphalt properties regardless of amount of rejuvenator applied, while the penetration test potentially identifies no change in asphalt property. The dynamic shear rheometer (DSR) test method is also used to produce results for evaluation; however, while the test requires less asphalt than the other methods, current extraction methods normally recover the amount of material required to perform the preferred viscosity test. If the DSR test method is used, select the phase angle test parameter for comparison since it has been shown to be statistically more consistent than the G* parameter.
key_points: Viscosity testing is more sensitive than penetration testing for detecting rejuvenator effects on asphalt binder.
The DSR test's phase angle parameter is statistically more consistent for this comparison than the G* parameter.
DSR testing requires less asphalt than other test methods, though current extraction methods usually recover enough for viscosity testing anyway.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the effectiveness of a rejuvenator treatment via laboratory binder testing.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Rejuvenation materials are unspecified by ASTM or other organizations and are proprietary, classified by major component as asphalt-based or coal-tar-based; performance should be verified by record or test area, and fog-sprayed emulsified asphalt does not qualify as a rejuvenator due to insufficient penetration.
sections.body: Rejuvenation materials are not currently specified by ASTM or any other organization. The various rejuvenators available are proprietary products. Available rejuvenator materials are classified into two major types according to their major components, either asphalt or coal tar bases. Ensure the rejuvenator selected for use has a proven record of performance; however, if performance data on a rejuvenator are not available, apply the rejuvenator to a test area on the pavement and evaluate to determine its potential performance. Fog spray applications of emulsified asphalt cannot be considered to act as a rejuvenator as they don't normally have significant penetration into the pavement surface.
key_points: Rejuvenators are proprietary, unspecified by ASTM; classified as asphalt-based or coal-tar-based.
Without a proven performance record, apply the rejuvenator to a test area first.
Fog-sprayed emulsified asphalt is NOT a substitute for a rejuvenator, since it lacks significant penetration.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and vetting a proprietary rejuvenator product for pavement use.

sections.title: Application Rate
sections.summary: Total liquid rejuvenator application rate is typically 0.18 to 0.9 liters per square meter (0.04 to 0.2 gallons per square yard), set by pavement absorption within 12-24 hours; rejuvenator-sealers additionally receive fine sand cover at about 0.27 to 0.54 kg/sq m (0.5 to 1.0 lb/sq yd) for initial skid resistance.
sections.body: The rate of application varies greatly with the condition (dry, oxidized, open-textured) of the pavement surface. Ensure the application rate of total liquid is within the range of 0.18 to 0.9 liters per square meter (0.04 to 0.2 gallons per square yard). The application rate is selected as the amount of material absorbed into the pavement surface within 12 to 24 hours of application, depending on the trafficking needs of the rejuvenated pavement. Follow the manufacturer's recommendations concerning dilution and other factors. Depending on the amount of solids or residual material within the rejuvenator, sand-sized aggregate is used to provide initial skid resistance after placement; rejuvenators that leave material on the surface to hold aggregate are classified as rejuvenator-sealers. The sand used is fine-grained, passing the 1.18 mm (No. 16) and usually the 600 micrometer (No. 30) sieve. The amount of aggregate applied varies with rejuvenator-sealer type and pavement condition, usually within 0.27 to 0.54 kilograms per square meter (0.5 to 1.0 pound per square yard).
key_points: Typical total-liquid rejuvenator application rate: 0.18-0.9 L/sq m (0.04-0.2 gal/sq yd).
Rate is set so material is absorbed into the pavement within 12-24 hours.
Rejuvenator-sealer sand cover passes the No. 16 (1.18 mm) and usually No. 30 (600 micrometer) sieve.
Rejuvenator-sealer sand application rate is typically 0.27-0.54 kg/sq m (0.5-1.0 lb/sq yd).
sections.applicability: Applies when setting rejuvenator liquid application rate and, for rejuvenator-sealers, the companion sand cover rate.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Rejuvenator is placed with an asphalt distributor truck or specialty spray vehicle onto a cleaned surface, sometimes with immediate aggregate application (rejuvenator-sealer); excess is blotted with clean dry sand and rolled with a rubber-tire roller 1-2 days later, applied above 10 C (50 F), with 21 C (70 F)+ giving improved penetration and curing.
sections.body: Prior to placement of the rejuvenator, thoroughly clean all the loose material from the pavement surface. Rejuvenators are usually placed with an asphalt distributor truck or any other type of specially designed application spray vehicle. Manufacturers and contractors have added a feature to immediately apply aggregate directly on top of the rejuvenator (rejuvenator-sealer). Follow manufacturer recommendations concerning application temperature and dilution. When a rejuvenator is applied, ensure clean dry sand is available to blot areas that received too much rejuvenator; spread the sand evenly, broom into a pile, and remove. Rolling the pavement surface with a rubber tire roller 1 or 2 days after rejuvenator application helps to knead and close hairline cracks. The minimum application temperature is normally 10 degrees C (50 degrees F); temperatures at or above 21 degrees C (70 degrees F) result in improved penetration and curing.
key_points: Minimum rejuvenator application temperature is 10 C (50 F); 21 C (70 F)+ improves penetration and curing.
Rejuvenator-sealers apply aggregate directly on top of the rejuvenator immediately after spraying.
Excess rejuvenator is blotted with clean dry sand.
Rubber-tire rolling 1-2 days after application helps knead and close hairline cracks.
sections.applicability: Applies to field placement procedure and temperature control for rejuvenator/rejuvenator-sealer application.

sections.title: Control
sections.summary: Rejuvenator control requires calibrating the asphalt distributor and checking nozzles per ASTM D2995; for rejuvenator-sealers, the aggregate distribution system is also calibrated and checked per ASTM D5624, with test sections used to verify application rates and equipment performance.
sections.body: Calibrate the asphalt distributor and check all nozzles according to ASTM D2995. When a rejuvenator-sealer is applied, the aggregate distribution system is calibrated and checked according to ASTM D5624. Conduct test sections of the pavement to be rejuvenated to test various application rates and the function of the distribution equipment.
key_points: Asphalt distributor calibration/nozzle checks follow ASTM D2995.
Rejuvenator-sealer aggregate distribution systems are calibrated/checked per ASTM D5624.
Test sections verify application rates and equipment function before full production.
sections.applicability: Applies to quality control checks on distributor and aggregate-spreading equipment for rejuvenator application.

sections.title: Skid Resistance
sections.summary: Rejuvenators normally reduce skid resistance, worsened by any unremoved excess; properly-dosed rejuvenator skid values approach pretreatment values within a few days, while rejuvenator-sealers rely on their aggregate cover for skid resistance until it wears off, after which skid resistance approaches the untreated pavement's value.
sections.body: Rejuvenators normally reduce the skid resistance of treated pavement surfaces. Any excess rejuvenator that is not removed reduces skid resistance further. Rejuvenator materials, when applied in the correct amounts, have skid resistance values approaching pretreatment values within a few days. Rejuvenator-sealer materials, those leaving substantial amounts of material on the pavement surface, provide skid resistance values when the application of aggregate has been applied to them. As the rejuvenator-sealer cures and traffic is applied, this thin layer of sand is worn off along with the material, and the skid resistance approaches that of the untreated pavement.
key_points: Rejuvenators reduce skid resistance initially; correctly-dosed treatments recover to near pretreatment values within a few days.
Unremoved excess rejuvenator further reduces skid resistance.
Rejuvenator-sealers depend on their aggregate cover for skid resistance until it wears off with traffic.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating skid resistance recovery timelines after rejuvenator or rejuvenator-sealer treatment.
